PyTorch currently has 139 test files1, 519 TestCase classes2, and 9984 test cases3. Some of these tests are already implicitly owned by internal teams, for example, the tests in the test/distributed folder are owned by the distributed team, but the ownership of other tests is more ambiguous.
Action
We should establish explicit test ownership to account for every test by linking groups of tests to PyTorch oncalls. Please comment on this RFC:

How should we establish explicit test ownership? Pick an option mentioned in the How section or suggest your own.
Please help link more tests to owners below!

Why?
Tests measure and reflect the functionality of PyTorch and promises a certain user experience. Flaky test signal confuses developers and prevents an accurate measure of trunk health, either leading developers to waste time investigating false positives or decreasing trunk reliability by obfuscating real issues.
Therefore, ensuring high test quality is crucial to developer and user experience, and we should stamp out bad quality tests as soon as possible. Just as developers fix buggy code according to their expertise, test owners would address broken or flaky tests as experts with the best context. When tests have owners, there is a strong case to keep them and rely on them as there is a guarantee that their quality will be maintained. On the flip side, it is harder to make the case to keep tests without owners, as their quality is not guaranteed.
Moreover, many tests already have implicit owners to whom people assign when the test requires attention! This RFC is not a novel idea but instead seeks to establish a clearer mapping so anyone can quickly know who to address when they have questions about a test.
How?
We want to maintain explicit mappings in a simple and enforceable way. The following options are inspired by already existing solutions we can easily extend.
Option 1: We can group test files into directories and modify the CODEOWNERS file to attribute directories to owners. This has also been put to use with /test/distributed and /test/onnx.
Option 2: We can add an entry in CODEOWNERS to attribute owners for every test file. A few teams have already utilized this, for example, with test_public_bindings.py and test_linalg.py.
Option 3 [the best option concluded from the discussion]: We can add a header to the top of every test file denoting the owner of the test file. This would be similar to how internal code utilizes file headers.
An option 4 would be adding decorators for every TestCase class or test case itself, but this option is inferior as it is more complicated and harder to enforce with a lint rule. I’ve started partitioning our test files into oncalls, but there are a lot more test files/directories to be claimed. Please comment to help attribute more of these tests to their proper owners! As for the leftover unowned tests, we can attribute them to a default owner of module: unknown when they are broken or flaky to allow this system to be complete.

🐛 Bug
The following code snippet fails on a source build on ARM (Neoverse N1) when the vectorized code path is triggered (tensor length >=16) when compiling with -O1 -fstrict-aliasing (or any higher optimization):
import torch
device = 'cpu'
size = 16
a = torch.full((size,), 6, dtype=torch.int32, device=device)
b = torch.full((size,), 3, dtype=torch.int32, device=device)
print(a & b)

tensor([    40960,         0,  46473216,     43691, 201326912,     43691,
                0,         0,     40960,         0,  46473216,     43691,
        201326912,     43691,         0,         0], dtype=torch.int32)
Expected output:
tensor([2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2], dtype=torch.int32)
TL;DR
Potential root cause
Strict aliasing rule violation in

  
    
      pytorch/aten/src/ATen/cpu/vec/vec_base.h
    
    
        Lines 742 to 743
      in
      2a5116e
    
  
  
    

        
          
           const intmax_t *a_ptr = reinterpret_cast<const intmax_t*>((const T*) a); 
        

        
          
           const intmax_t *b_ptr = reinterpret_cast<const intmax_t*>((const T*) b); 
        
    
  


Fix could be
template<class T, typename Op>
static inline Vectorized<T> bitwise_binary_op(const Vectorized<T> &a, const Vectorized<T> &b, Op op) {
  static constexpr uint32_t element_no = VECTOR_WIDTH / sizeof(intmax_t);
  __at_align__ intmax_t buffer[element_no];
  intmax_t a_ptr[element_no]; // !
  intmax_t b_ptr[element_no]; // !
  std::memcpy(&a_ptr, &a, sizeof(intmax_t) * element_no); // !
  std::memcpy(&b_ptr, &b, sizeof(intmax_t) * element_no); // !
  for (uint32_t i = 0U; i < element_no; ++ i) {
    buffer[i] = op(a_ptr[i], b_ptr[i]);
  }
  return Vectorized<T>::loadu(buffer);
}
Reference: What is the Strict Aliasing Rule and Why do we care? by @shafik
We've verified this fix locally on tensor shapes in arange(1, 1280), but please add others as needed to check, if the proposed fix is valid or not.
Details
Vectorized code path
We've seen unit test failures on ARM nodes for bitwise_and operations and first narrowed it down to the vectorized code path, as all sizes <16 work as expected and to optimized code (-O0 did not reproduce this issue and we needed to rebuild with REL_WITH_DEB_INFO=1).
Heisenbug
While trying to further isolate the issue it turned out to be a Heisenbug, which "disappeared" once we looked too close into the functions in question.
E.g. by adding a std::cout here:

  
    
      pytorch/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/BinaryOpsKernel.cpp
    
    
         Line 258
      in
      94d6215
    
  
  
    

        
          
           return a & b; 
        
    
  


the method worked correctly again. Also, gdb refused to step into

  
    
      pytorch/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/Loops.h
    
    
        Lines 216 to 217
      in
      c5bee1e
    
  
  
    

        
          
           auto out1 = c10::guts::apply(std::forward<vec_func_t>(vop), std::move(args1)); 
        

        
          
           auto out2 = c10::guts::apply(std::forward<vec_func_t>(vop), std::move(args2)); 
        
    
  


or break in bitwise_binary_op, but we were unsure, if this is due to the release + debug symbols build or not.
Adding a raise(SIGTRAP) in bitwise_binary_op also restored the functionality again.
As the next step we've used
template<class T, typename Op>
static inline Vectorized<T> __attribute__((optimize("O0"))) bitwise_binary_op(const Vectorized<T> &a, const Vectorized<T> &b, Op op) {
to disable any optimizations in this method to be able to step into it via gdb, but this of course also fixed the issue (it also turns out that __attribute((optimize("-fno-strict-aliasing"))) is also a valid workaround).
valgrind --track-origins=yes also confirmed the usage of uninitialized memory in at::native::bitwise_and_kernel in the failing cases and wasn't reporting issues otherwise.
Bisecting compiler opimization flags
This lead us to the assumption, that one of the optimizations might trigger the failure and we bisected it to -O1 -fstrict-aliasing.
After reading @shafik's great blog post (I would highly recommend reading it in case you are interested why the linked type punning is invalid) we realized that the vectorized code path might indeed violate the strict aliasing rule.
Replacing the (invalid) reinterpret_cast with the memcpy restores the behavior.
Why no failures on x86/AVX?
It's a bit unclear why this issue was only visible on this particular ARM node as vec_base.h seems to use the invalid reinterpret_cast in more places (in AVX code) so this issue should also have been visible on x86 (we might also want to check and fix it).
NIT
It seems that -Wno-strict-aliasing is used

  
    
      pytorch/CMakeLists.txt
    
    
         Line 751
      in
      2a5116e
    
  
  
    

        
          
           string(APPEND CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS " -Wno-strict-aliasing") 
        
    
  


in combination with -O2

  
    
      pytorch/CMakeLists.txt
    
    
         Line 734
      in
      2a5116e
    
  
  
    

        
          
           string(APPEND CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS " -O2 -fPIC") 
        
    
  


which seems dangerous, as it would disable the warnings while the compiler could still use this optimization.

🚀 Feature

The autograd profiler has a config option called report_input_shapes this option causes the input tensor shapes of each operator to appear in the nvtx range of each op.  The sequence_nr, or unique id, of each operator is also reported in the nvtx range next to the tensor shapes.  This information is very useful for performance analysis, however in addition to the tensor shapes and sequence_nr it is also useful to know which operators produced the input tensors.  With this information the end user can reconstruct the network graph, which is otherwise quite difficult to get from PyTorch.   This feature request is asking that the sequence_nr of the nodes that produced each input tensor is recorded and made available to the profiler and reported in the nvtx range.  When the inputSizes() function is called, another function can be called to return the list of sequence_nr's which produced the tensors represented by the inputSizes() function.
Motivation

I do performance analysis of PyTorch networks for my job at Nvidia and one of the main things I need to be able to do is to map each GPU kernel to the unique instance of the PyTorch op that launched it.  In addition I want to see where the op is in the network graph, a descriptive unique instance name, the tensor dimensions, parameters and op type are for each op.  The information available to the  profiler is quite good today, but is still a challenge to map back to the higher level PyTorch front end.
Pitch

I have actually implemented this feature already in a copy of PyTorch that is maintained internally at Nvidia.  I have also implemented software that parses the output of the profiler and generates a network graph visualization based on the sequence_nr and input sequence_nr's as proposed above.  I would like to make these changes available to the PyTorch community.
Alternatives

We used to rely on a third party extension called PyProf which was used to capture some of the information listed above.  This software proved to be really error prone and required a lot of maintenance.  The proposed solution is simpler and less error prone as it relies on native PyTorch features.
Additional context
The below timeline view shows the input sequence id numbers (seq_ids) and the sequence_nr (seq) of the aten::cudnn_convolution_op().  The user can follow the input seq_ids to find the ops that produced both the input activation and weight tensor.  The unique seq id of the node coupled with the input seq_ids to the node are all you need to construct the network graph.


Here's a screenshot from a network graph that was generated using the proposed feature.

📚 Documentation
Seeing the torch.angle() description (https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.angle.html), it says that the behavior of torch.angle() has been changed since 1.8.0. Following is the note from the link.
====== Note =======
Starting in PyTorch 1.8, angle returns pi for negative real numbers, zero for non-negative real numbers, and propagates NaNs. Previously the function would return zero for all real numbers and not propagate floating-point NaNs.
Here, I don't understand what it means by 'propagates NaNs'. I understood it as its gradient will be NaN when the input to Torch.angle() is real value. However, when I tested, it seems its gradient is not Nan.
    x1=torch.tensor([[0, 4, -4, 1+4j]], dtype=torch.cfloat, requires_grad=True)
    out = x1.angle()
    print(out)
    out.mean().backward()
    print(x1.grad)

    tensor([[0.0000, 0.0000, 3.1416, 1.3258]], grad_fn=<AngleBackward>)
    tensor([[ 0.0000+0.0000j,  0.0000+0.0625j, -0.0000-0.0625j, -0.0588+0.0147j]])

If my understanding to the note is correct, the gradient from angle() when its input is real value should be Nan, but it is not.
Could anyone help me understand when torch.angle() returns Nan as its gradient? Or is my understanding on the documentation is wrong?

def _safe_norm(v):
    if not torch.isfinite(v).all():

def line_search(update, x0, g0, g, nstep=0, on=True):
    """
    `update` is the propsoed direction of update.

    Code adapted from scipy.
    """
    tmp_s = [0]
    tmp_g0 = [g0]
    tmp_phi = [torch.norm(g0)**2]
    s_norm = torch.norm(x0) / torch.norm(update)

    def phi(s, store=True):
        if s == tmp_s[0]:
            return tmp_phi[0]    # If the step size is so small... just return something
        x_est = x0 + s * update
        g0_new = g(x_est)
        phi_new = _safe_norm(g0_new)**2
        if store:
            tmp_s[0] = s
            tmp_g0[0] = g0_new
            tmp_phi[0] = phi_new
        return phi_new
    
    if on:
        pass

        ite = 0

    x_est = x0 + s * update
    if s == tmp_s[0]:

    else:

    return x_est, g0_new, x_est - x0, g0_new - g0, ite

def rmatvec(part_Us, part_VTs, x):
    # Compute x^T(-I + UV^T)
    # x: (N, 2d, L')
    # part_Us: (N, 2d, L', threshold)
    # part_VTs: (N, threshold, 2d, L')
    if part_Us.nelement() == 0:
        return -x
    xTU = torch.einsum('bij, bijd -> bd', x, part_Us)   # (N, threshold)
    return -x + torch.einsum('bd, bdij -> bij', xTU, part_VTs)    # (N, 2d, L'), but should really be (N, 1, (2d*L'))

def matvec(part_Us, part_VTs, x):
    # Compute (-I + UV^T)x
    # x: (N, 2d, L')
    # part_Us: (N, 2d, L', threshold)
    # part_VTs: (N, threshold, 2d, L')
    if part_Us.nelement() == 0:
        return -x
    VTx = torch.einsum('bdij, bij -> bd', part_VTs, x)  # (N, threshold)
    return -x + torch.einsum('bijd, bd -> bij', part_Us, VTx)     # (N, 2d, L'), but should really be (N, (2d*L'), 1)

def broyden(f, x0, threshold, eps=1e-3, stop_mode="rel", ls=False, name="unknown"):
    bsz, total_hsize, seq_len = x0.size()
    g = lambda y: f(y) - y
    dev = x0.device
    alternative_mode = 'rel' if stop_mode == 'abs' else 'abs'
    
    x_est = x0           # (bsz, 2d, L')
    gx = g(x_est)        # (bsz, 2d, L')
    nstep = 0
    tnstep = 0
    
    # For fast calculation of inv_jacobian (approximately)
    Us = torch.zeros(bsz, total_hsize, seq_len, threshold).to(dev) # One can also use an L-BFGS scheme to further reduce memory
    VTs = torch.zeros(bsz, threshold, total_hsize, seq_len).to(dev)
    update = -matvec(Us[:,:,:,:nstep], VTs[:,:nstep], gx)      # Formally should be -torch.matmul(inv_jacobian (-I), gx)
    prot_break = False
    
    # To be used in protective breaks
    protect_thres = (1e6 if stop_mode == "abs" else 1e3) * seq_len
    new_objective = 1e8

    trace_dict = {'abs': [],
                  'rel': []}
    lowest_dict = {'abs': 1e8,
                   'rel': 1e8}
    lowest_step_dict = {'abs': 0,
                        'rel': 0}
    nstep, lowest_xest, lowest_gx = 0, x_est, gx

    while nstep < threshold:
        x_est, gx, delta_x, delta_gx, ite = line_search(update, x_est, gx, g, nstep=nstep, on=ls)
        nstep += 1
        tnstep += (ite+1)
        abs_diff = torch.norm(gx).item()
        rel_diff = abs_diff / (torch.norm(gx + x_est).item() + 1e-9)
        diff_dict = {'abs': abs_diff,
                     'rel': rel_diff}
        trace_dict['abs'].append(abs_diff)
        trace_dict['rel'].append(rel_diff)
        for mode in ['rel', 'abs']:
            if diff_dict[mode] < lowest_dict[mode]:
                if mode == stop_mode: 
                    lowest_xest, lowest_gx = x_est.clone().detach(), gx.clone().detach()
                lowest_dict[mode] = diff_dict[mode]
                lowest_step_dict[mode] = nstep

        new_objective = diff_dict[stop_mode]
        if new_objective < eps: break
        if new_objective < 3*eps and nstep > 30 and np.max(trace_dict[stop_mode][-30:]) / np.min(trace_dict[stop_mode][-30:]) < 1.3:
            # if there's hardly been any progress in the last 30 steps
            break
        if new_objective > trace_dict[stop_mode][0] * protect_thres:
            prot_break = True
            break

        part_Us, part_VTs = Us[:,:,:,:nstep-1], VTs[:,:nstep-1]

        vT[vT != vT] = 0
        u[u != u] = 0
        VTs[:,nstep-1] = vT
        Us[:,:,:,nstep-1] = u
        update = -matvec(Us[:,:,:,:nstep], VTs[:,:nstep], gx)

    for _ in range(threshold+1-len(trace_dict[stop_mode])):
        trace_dict[stop_mode].append(lowest_dict[stop_mode])
        trace_dict[alternative_mode].append(lowest_dict[alternative_mode])

    return {"result": lowest_xest,
            "lowest": lowest_dict[stop_mode],
            "nstep": lowest_step_dict[stop_mode],
            "prot_break": prot_break,
            "abs_trace": trace_dict['abs'],
            "rel_trace": trace_dict['rel'],

def tensor2vec(x):
    b = x.shape[0]

    b = x.shape[0]

class ResNetLayer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_channels, n_inner_channels, kernel_size=3, num_groups=8):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(n_channels, n_inner_channels, kernel_size, padding=kernel_size//2, bias=False)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(n_inner_channels, n_channels, kernel_size, padding=kernel_size//2, bias=False)
        self.norm1 = nn.GroupNorm(num_groups, n_inner_channels)
        self.norm2 = nn.GroupNorm(num_groups, n_channels)
        self.norm3 = nn.GroupNorm(num_groups, n_channels)
        self.conv1.weight.data.normal_(0, 0.01)
        self.conv2.weight.data.normal_(0, 0.01)
        
    def forward(self, z, x):
        y = self.norm1(F.relu(self.conv1(z)))
        return self.norm3(F.relu(z + self.norm2(x + self.conv2(y))))


class DEQModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, f, solver, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.f = f
        self.solver = solver
        self.kwargs = kwargs
        self.hook = None
        self.removed_hooks = []
    
    def forward(self, x):
        # Preparation
        _, c, h, w = x.shape
        z0 = tensor2vec(torch.zeros_like(x))  # initial z state is zero
        func = lambda z: tensor2vec(self.f(vec2tensor(z, (c, h, w)), x))

        # Forward pass. Solve for fixed point of f -> z_star.
        with torch.no_grad():
            z_star = self.solver(func, z0, **self.kwargs)['result']

        # Backward pass
        if self.training:
            # re-engage autograd tape
            z_star_old = z_star.requires_grad_()
            z_star = func(z_star_old)

            def backward_hook(grad):
                if self.hook is not None:
                    self.hook.remove()  # To avoid infinite recursion when calling autograd.grad(z_star, ...)
                    # remove_hook(self.hook, self.removed_hooks) # uncomment to use custom remove hook function
                    torch.cuda.synchronize()
                # Compute the fixed point of yJ + grad, where J=J_f is the Jacobian of f at z_star
                # look at http://implicit-layers-tutorial.org/deep_equilibrium_models/
                grad_func = lambda y: autograd.grad(z_star, z_star_old, y, retain_graph=True)[0] + grad
                new_grad = self.solver(grad_func, torch.zeros_like(grad), **self.kwargs)['result']
                return new_grad

            self.hook = z_star.register_hook(backward_hook)
        return vec2tensor(z_star, (c, h, w))

    # Models
    f = ResNetLayer(64, 128)
    deq = DEQModel(f, broyden, threshold=30, stop_mode='abs', eps=1e-3)

Right now, there's a many-to-one correspondence between entries in native_functions.yaml and functions in torch.ops; specifically, all overloads get mapped to a single torch.ops function. For example, add.Tensor and add.out both show up as torch.ops.aten.add.
This is problematic for the introspection track of primtorch, because the metadata associated with various operators may vary across overloads. As a simple example, in #64874 the user wants to know what the mutable arguments are for the function, but they cannot figure this out without looking at the keyword arguments, because both add.Tensor (which doesn't mutate) and add.out (which does mutate) both get mapped to the same func (torch.ops.aten.add).
The proposal is to add support for indexing on functions in torch.ops that resolve them to a specific overload. So torch.ops.aten.add represents all overloads of add, but torch.ops.aten.add["Tensor"] represents only the add.Tensor overload. You can index with the empty string, e.g., torch.ops.aten.addmv[""] in cases where the overload has no overload name.
With this variant, you now can easily attach schema and other annotations on the overloaded functions without any ambiguity, and this makes it easier to do introspection. We also suggest changing __torch_dispatch__ to accept overloads by default (BC-breaking) rather than overload bundles (traditional torch.ops.aten.add); as you can always recover the overload bundle from the overload (perhaps some property like torch.ops.aten.add["Tensor"].parent). Alternately, we introduce a new magic method __torch_dispatch_ex__ that accepts overloads instead of overload bundles.
With this change, we can also offer default argument resolution easily (e.g., please give me the default values for all positional arguments). Previously, this was not easy to do because we would have had to redo overload resolution to understand what positional arguments we'd be getting.
Downside of this proposal: overload names are hypothetically not supposed to be part of public API, this change makes them visible from Python and BC concerns now apply to them. (This was already true for eager mode extensions).

An alternate proposal, is to introduce a new variant of torch.ops, maybe torch.ops.variants which distinguish between overloads. So you would have torch.ops.aten.add['Tensor'] and torch.ops.variants.aten.out (note: we cannot reuse torch.ops.aten for variants with no overload name, as it is ambiguous in some cases; e.g., addmv has addmv (no overload name) and addmv.out (overload name); if I gave you torch.ops.aten.addmv, you would not be able to tell if this was representing all overloads (as is the legacy behavior) or just addmv (no overload name)).
cc @albanD

Answering whether a GPU is being used or not throws off beginners and advanced users alike who will run things like
import torch
torch.cuda.is_available()

And then device = torch.device("cuda:0" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
And need to double check that all tensors are on the GPU by writing something like tensor.to(device) since Pytorch doesn't send tensors to GPUs by default if its available
And ultimately you either know if your GPU is being used or not by either checking if a model feels too slowly or going to nvidia-smi
Pitch
`torch.cuda.utilization() -> 99%
`torch.cuda.memory_usage() -> 30%

nvidia-smi is great but people need this data at runtime in their code, if a model wasn't loaded to GPU stop. Or GPU utlization is too low, restart job with a larger batch size
We could just do a grep search on top os.system('nvidia-smi') and capture that in functions or maybe there's some fancier way to do this that doesns't involve grepping
Maybe this needs more thought in distributed settings but for now we can limit scope to single node
Alternatives
This gap is already met by a bunch of tools like

https://github.com/anderskm/gputil
https://github.com/rossumai/nvgpu

But those tools provide comprehensive information. We just need to help deep learning practitioners  debug their issues namely: Are you using your GPU? And are you using your GPU to its full capacity?

🐛 Bug
torch.onnx.export() fails to export the model that contains customized function. According to the following documentation, the custom operator should be exported as is if operator_export_type is set to ONNX_FALLTHROUGH:
torch doc
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Run the following simplified python code:

import torch

class MyRelu(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, input):
        ctx.save_for_backward(input)
        return input.clamp(min=0)

    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_output):
        input, = ctx.saved_tensors
        grad_input = grad_output.clone()
        grad_input[input < 0] = 0
        return grad_input

class MyModule(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(MyModule, self).__init__()
        
    def forward(self, input):
        return MyRelu.apply(input)
    
module = MyModule()
x = torch.randn(5, 5)
y = module(x)

torch.onnx.export(module, x, 'test.onnx', export_params=True, opset_version=13, operator_export_type=torch.onnx.OperatorExportTypes.ONNX_FALLTHROUGH, do_constant_folding=False, verbose=False, input_names=['input'], output_names=['output'])

This is a bootcamp issue for the roll-up here: #48845.
PyTorch supports laying out tensor data in multiple different memory formats. Specifically, channels_last is a different memory format that's been shown to speed up kernels on the GPU. See https://pytorch.org/tutorials/intermediate/memory_format_tutorial.html for more details.
channel_last memory format support needs to be added individually for each operator though, and not all ops are covered. For this issue, add a memory_format kwarg to torch.zeros(). The following should work after the change:
import torch
a = torch.zeros((2,2,2,2), memory_format=torch.channels_last)

The files that you'll have to change include:

aten/src/ATen/native_functions.yaml: this is the entry-point to our codegen pipeline, and includes JIT schemas for every native operator. The python bindings and C++ API for each operator are generated from here
aten/src/ATen/native/TensorFactories.cpp contains the C++ implementation, under the namespace at::native::zeros. In this case, torch.zeros is a composite operator, so there's only one implementation (and not, say, a separate cpu and cuda kernel).

Although there is no definition of L norms for complex inputs (or at least I didn't find any), our current implementation of the L1 norm is probably not doing what a user would expect:

  
    
      pytorch/aten/src/ATen/native/Loss.cpp
    
    
         Line 499
      in
      facff2e
    
  
  
    

        
          
           auto loss = diff.is_complex() ? diff.abs() : diff.abs_(); 
        
    
  


abs(diff) is fine for real inputs, but for complex inputs this is equivalent to sqrt((input.real - target.real) ** 2 + (input.imag - target.imag) ** 2). This closely resembles the L2 norm rather the L1 norm.
A version probably more aligned with the user expectation, would be to perform the abs(diff) componentwise and sum up the results.
